subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 came into force with effect from 1 January 1974 and was repealed and replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 with effect from-

options.A: 1 April 1999
options.B: 1 January 2000
options.C: 1 April 2001
options.D: 1 June 2000

answer_html:
Answer: (D) 1 June 2000.

A system of exchange control was first introduced through rules under the Defence of India Act, 1939 on a temporary basis, and the first statute was the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 came into force with effect from January 1, 1974 and regulated foreign exchange for more than 26 years. After the liberalization policy of 1991 and the Tarapore Committee on Capital Account Convertibility constituted by the Reserve Bank in 1997, the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 took effect from June 01, 2000.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 was formulated with a total of-

options.A: 47 sections divided into 5 chapters
options.B: 46 sections divided into 9 chapters
options.C: 59 sections divided into 7 chapters
options.D: 49 sections divided into 7 chapters

answer_html:
Answer: (D) 49 sections divided into 7 chapters.

The Act was formulated with a total of 49 sections divided into 7 chapters. The legal framework also comprises 5 sets of Rules made by the Ministry under Section 46, 23 sets of Regulations made by the Reserve Bank under Section 47, master circulars and directions issued by the Reserve Bank, the foreign direct investment policy, and notifications and A.P. (DIR Series) circulars.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999-

options.A: both Rules and Regulations are made by the Ministry, the Reserve Bank issuing only circulars and directions
options.B: Rules are made by the Ministry under Section 46 and Regulations are made by the Reserve Bank under Section 47
options.C: Rules are made by the Reserve Bank under Section 46 and Regulations are made by the Ministry under Section 47
options.D: both Rules and Regulations are made by the Reserve Bank, under Sections 46 and 47 respectively of the Act

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Rules are made by the Ministry under Section 46 and Regulations are made by the Reserve Bank under Section 47.

The framework consists of the Act itself as the supreme legislation, 5 sets of Rules made by the Ministry under Section 46 of the Act as delegated legislation, and 23 sets of Regulations made by the Reserve Bank under Section 47 as subordinate legislation. Master circulars and directions, the foreign direct investment policy, and notifications and A.P. (DIR Series) circulars issued by the Reserve Bank complete the framework.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The scheme of the Act is that-

options.A: capital account transactions are deemed permitted unless expressly restricted, while current account transactions need to be expressly permitted
options.B: both current and capital account transactions are deemed permitted unless the Reserve Bank expressly restricts them by regulation
options.C: both current and capital account transactions require express permission, whether of the Central Government or of the Reserve Bank
options.D: current account transactions are deemed permitted unless expressly restricted, while capital account transactions need to be expressly permitted

answer_html:
Answer: (D) current account transactions are deemed permitted unless expressly restricted, while capital account transactions need to be expressly permitted.

Whereas the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act sought to regulate everything specified, the Foreign Exchange Management Act lays down that everything other than what is expressly covered is not controlled. Current account transactions are deemed permitted unless expressly specified, and in respect of capital account transactions they need to be expressly permitted to be transacted. Section 5 removes restrictions on the withdrawal of foreign exchange for the purpose of current account transactions.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A person resident in India means, among others, a person residing in India for more than-

options.A: 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year
options.B: 182 days during the course of the current financial year
options.C: 90 days during the course of the preceding financial year
options.D: 365 days during the course of the two preceding financial years

answer_html:
Answer: (A) 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year.

A person resident in India means a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year, but does not include a person who has gone out of or stays outside India for employment, for carrying on a business or vocation, or in circumstances indicating an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period, nor a person who has come to or stays in India otherwise than for those purposes. The expression also covers any person or body corporate registered or incorporated in India, an office, branch or agency in India owned or controlled by a person resident outside India, and an office, branch or agency outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: While the Reserve Bank may, in consultation with the Central Government, specify the permissible classes of capital account transactions and the limits for them, it shall not impose any restriction on the drawal of foreign exchange for payments due on account of-

options.A: the transfer of a foreign security by a person resident in India to a person resident outside India
options.B: the guarantee or surety given by a resident where a foreign exchange transaction is involved in it
options.C: amortisation of loans or depreciation of direct investments in the ordinary course of business
options.D: the acquisition of immovable property outside India by a person resident in India

answer_html:
Answer: (C) amortisation of loans or depreciation of direct investments in the ordinary course of business.

Any person may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person for a capital account transaction, subject to the Reserve Bank specifying, in consultation with the Central Government, the permissible classes of such transactions and the limits up to which foreign exchange is admissible. The proviso to Section 6 nevertheless bars the Reserve Bank from imposing any restriction on the drawal of foreign exchange for payments due on account of amortisation of loans or for depreciation of direct investments in the ordinary course of business.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Foreign direct investment is prohibited in-

options.A: Nidhi company, trading in Transferable Development Rights, and real estate investment trusts registered with SEBI
options.B: gambling and betting including casinos, the construction of roads and bridges, and the manufacture of pharmaceuticals
options.C: lottery business, gambling and betting including casinos, Nidhi company and trading in Transferable Development Rights
options.D: lottery business, gambling and betting including casinos, and the development of townships and residential premises

answer_html:
Answer: (C) lottery business, gambling and betting including casinos, Nidhi company and trading in Transferable Development Rights.

Foreign direct investment is prohibited in lottery business including Government and private lotteries and online lotteries, gambling and betting including casinos, chit funds except for investment by non-resident Indians and overseas citizens of India on a non-repatriation basis, Nidhi company, trading in Transferable Development Rights, real estate business or the construction of farm houses, the manufacture of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes of tobacco or tobacco substitutes, and activities not open to private sector investment, namely atomic energy and railway operations other than the permitted activities. Real estate business does not include the development of townships, the construction of residential or commercial premises, roads or bridges, or real estate investment trusts registered under the SEBI Regulations, 2014.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under the entry routes for foreign investment-

options.A: the automatic route requires prior Government approval, while the Government route requires no approval where the sectoral cap is not exceeded
options.B: both routes require the prior approval of the Reserve Bank, the difference being only in the time within which that approval is granted
options.C: the automatic route requires no prior approval of the Reserve Bank or of the Government, while the Government route requires prior Government approval
options.D: the automatic route requires the prior approval of the Reserve Bank, while the Government route requires the prior approval of the Central Government

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the automatic route requires no prior approval of the Reserve Bank or of the Government, while the Government route requires prior Government approval.

The automatic route does not require the prior approval of the Reserve Bank or of the Government. The Government route is the entry route which requires prior Government approval, and the concerned ministry gives that approval. Foreign investment is permitted up to 100% on the automatic route in sectors or activities not listed in the relevant regulation and not prohibited.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The capital instruments through which foreign direct investment may be made in an Indian company are-

options.A: equity shares, preference shares and any deposit accepted by the Indian company from a non-resident
options.B: equity shares, debentures, preference shares and share warrants issued by the Indian company
options.C: equity shares and preference shares alone, no form of debenture or warrant being a capital instrument
options.D: equity shares, debentures and any instrument of debt issued by the Indian company to a non-resident

answer_html:
Answer: (B) equity shares, debentures, preference shares and share warrants issued by the Indian company.

The capital instruments are equity shares, debentures, preference shares and share warrants issued by the Indian company. Instruments which are fully convertible, namely fully convertible debentures and fully convertible preference shares, are also treated as capital instruments; instruments which are not fully and mandatorily convertible are treated as debt.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Where partly paid equity shares are issued to a person resident outside India-

options.A: the whole of the consideration including share premium must be received upfront, partly paid shares being otherwise prohibited
options.B: twenty five per cent of the total consideration including share premium must be received upfront and the balance within twelve months
options.C: fifty per cent of the total consideration including share premium must be received upfront and the balance within twelve months
options.D: twenty five per cent of the total consideration excluding share premium must be received upfront and the balance within six months

answer_html:
Answer: (B) twenty five per cent of the total consideration including share premium must be received upfront and the balance within twelve months.

Twenty five per cent of the total consideration amount, including the share premium if any, has to be received upfront, and the balance consideration towards fully paid equity shares should be received within a period of twelve months from the date of issue of the partly paid shares.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: As regards investment by citizens of, or entities incorporated in, Bangladesh and Pakistan-

options.A: both require prior Government approval, and a Bangladeshi investor may not invest in defence, space, atomic energy or the prohibited sectors at all
options.B: both may invest under the automatic route, save that a Pakistani investor requires prior Government approval in the defence sector alone
options.C: neither may invest in India in any sector or activity whatsoever, whether under the automatic route or with Government approval
options.D: both require prior Government approval, and a Pakistani investor may not invest in defence, space, atomic energy or the prohibited sectors at all

answer_html:
Answer: (D) both require prior Government approval, and a Pakistani investor may not invest in defence, space, atomic energy or the prohibited sectors at all.

Any investment by a person who is a citizen of Bangladesh or Pakistan, or by an entity incorporated in Bangladesh or Pakistan, requires prior Government approval. A person who is a citizen of Pakistan, or an entity incorporated in Pakistan, can invest only with prior Government approval and only in sectors or activities other than defence, space, atomic energy and the sectors or activities prohibited for foreign investment.

question_html: The minimum average maturity period prescribed under the external commercial borrowing framework is-

options.A: 3 years
options.B: 1 year
options.C: 5 years
options.D: 7 years

answer_html:
Answer: (A) 3 years.

The framework prescribes a minimum average maturity period of 3 years. External commercial borrowings may be raised in foreign currency or in Indian Rupees, and the forms include loans including bank loans, floating or fixed rate notes, bonds and debentures other than fully and compulsorily convertible instruments, trade credits beyond 3 years, and financial lease.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Where foreign currency denominated external commercial borrowing is raised from a direct foreign equity holder, the ECB liability to equity ratio under the automatic route cannot exceed-

options.A: 7:1, and that ratio applies in every case whatever the outstanding amount of the borrowings of the entity may happen to be
options.B: 2:1, and that ratio does not apply where the outstanding amount of all such borrowing including the proposed one is up to USD 50 million
options.C: 7:1, and that ratio does not apply where the outstanding amount of all such borrowing including the proposed one is up to USD 5 million
options.D: 4:1, and that ratio does not apply where the outstanding amount of all such borrowing including the proposed one is up to USD 5 million

answer_html:
Answer: (C) 7:1, and that ratio does not apply where the outstanding amount of all such borrowing including the proposed one is up to USD 5 million.

For foreign currency denominated external commercial borrowing raised from a direct foreign equity holder, the ECB liability to equity ratio for borrowing raised under the automatic route cannot exceed 7:1. That ratio is not applicable if the outstanding amount of all external commercial borrowings, including the proposed one, is up to USD 5 million or its equivalent. Borrowing entities are also governed by any guidelines on debt equity ratio issued by the sectoral or prudential regulator concerned.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following correctly states the position on external commercial borrowings?

options.A: The proceeds cannot be used for investment in the capital market, and must in every case be parked abroad until they are actually utilised for the stated purpose
options.B: The proceeds cannot be used for real estate activities, investment in the capital market or equity investment, and may be parked in term deposits with AD Category I banks for a maximum of 12 months cumulatively
options.C: The proceeds cannot be used for real estate activities alone, and may be parked in term deposits with AD Category I banks for a maximum period of 24 months cumulatively from receipt
options.D: The proceeds may be used for any purpose whatever, but may not be parked in term deposits with AD Category I banks in India at any time before their utilisation

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The proceeds cannot be used for real estate activities, investment in the capital market or equity investment, and may be parked in term deposits with AD Category I banks for a maximum of 12 months cumulatively.

The negative list of end uses includes real estate activities, investment in capital market and equity investment, as well as on-lending to entities for those activities. Proceeds meant only for foreign currency expenditure can be parked abroad pending utilisation and may till then be invested in a few specified liquid assets, while proceeds meant for Rupee expenditure should be repatriated immediately for credit to the borrower's Rupee accounts with AD Category I banks in India, and may also be parked in term deposits with such banks for a maximum period of 12 months cumulatively.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme all resident individuals, including minors, are allowed to freely remit-

options.A: up to USD 25,000 per financial year for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both
options.B: up to USD 2,50,000 per calendar year, but only for permissible current account transactions and not for capital account ones
options.C: any amount whatever for permissible current account transactions, capital account transactions being outside the Scheme
options.D: up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both

answer_html:
Answer: (D) up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both.

All resident individuals, including minors, are allowed to freely remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year, that is April to March, for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both. The Scheme was introduced on February 4, 2004 with a limit of USD 25,000, and the limit has been revised in stages consistent with prevailing macro and micro economic conditions.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Mr Kartik Rao is a resident individual who has maintained his bank account with an Authorised Dealer Category I bank for the past four years.

During the financial year 2026-27 he has already remitted USD 90,000 towards the studies of his daughter abroad and USD 60,000 as a gift to a close relative who is a non-resident Indian.

He now proposes to remit a further USD 80,000 towards the purchase of a flat overseas. He also wishes to draw foreign exchange under the Scheme for a private visit to Nepal, and his spouse, who will not be a co-owner of the flat, wishes to club her own limit with his for the purchase.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The proposed remittance of USD 80,000 towards the purchase of the flat-

options.A: is within the Scheme, USD 100,000 of the annual limit remaining unutilised after the earlier remittances
options.B: is outside the Scheme, the earlier remittances having exhausted the whole of the annual limit available
options.C: is outside the Scheme, the purchase of immovable property abroad being prohibited under the Scheme
options.D: is within the Scheme, but only if the prior permission of the Reserve Bank is obtained before remitting

answer_html:
Answer: (A) is within the Scheme, USD 100,000 of the annual limit remaining unutilised after the earlier remittances.

The total amount of foreign exchange purchased from or remitted through all sources in India during a financial year must be within the cumulative limit of USD 2,50,000. Mr Rao has already remitted USD 90,000 and USD 60,000, that is USD 150,000 in all, leaving USD 100,000 of the limit unutilised, so the proposed remittance of USD 80,000 is within the Scheme. There are no restrictions on the frequency of remittances under the Scheme.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Mr Kartik Rao is a resident individual who has maintained his bank account with an Authorised Dealer Category I bank for the past four years.

During the financial year 2026-27 he has already remitted USD 90,000 towards the studies of his daughter abroad and USD 60,000 as a gift to a close relative who is a non-resident Indian.

He now proposes to remit a further USD 80,000 towards the purchase of a flat overseas. He also wishes to draw foreign exchange under the Scheme for a private visit to Nepal, and his spouse, who will not be a co-owner of the flat, wishes to club her own limit with his for the purchase.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The wish of the spouse to club her limit with that of Mr Rao for the purchase of the flat-

options.A: cannot be given effect to, clubbing being impermissible for a capital account transaction such as the purchase of property where she is not a co-owner
options.B: can be given effect to, remittances under the facility being capable of consolidation in respect of close family members in every case whatever
options.C: can be given effect to, provided the Authorised Dealer satisfies itself as to the source of the funds remitted by each of the two spouses
options.D: cannot be given effect to, the consolidation of remittances by close family members being impermissible for any purpose under the Scheme

answer_html:
Answer: (A) cannot be given effect to, clubbing being impermissible for a capital account transaction such as the purchase of property where she is not a co-owner.

Remittances under the facility can be consolidated in respect of close family members, subject to the individual family members complying with the terms and conditions of the Scheme. Clubbing is not, however, permitted by other family members for capital account transactions such as opening a bank account, investment or the purchase of property, if they are not the co-owners or co-partners of the investment, property or overseas bank account.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Mr Kartik Rao is a resident individual who has maintained his bank account with an Authorised Dealer Category I bank for the past four years.

During the financial year 2026-27 he has already remitted USD 90,000 towards the studies of his daughter abroad and USD 60,000 as a gift to a close relative who is a non-resident Indian.

He now proposes to remit a further USD 80,000 towards the purchase of a flat overseas. He also wishes to draw foreign exchange under the Scheme for a private visit to Nepal, and his spouse, who will not be a co-owner of the flat, wishes to club her own limit with his for the purchase.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. If Mr Rao remits the full amount of USD 2,50,000 during the financial year and the proceeds of an overseas investment are afterwards brought back into India within the same year, he-

options.A: may remit afresh without limit, the annual ceiling applying only to the first remittance of the year
options.B: is not eligible to make any further remittance under the Scheme during that financial year
options.C: becomes eligible to remit afresh to the extent of the amount brought back into the country
options.D: becomes eligible to remit afresh to the extent of one half of the amount brought back to India

answer_html:
Answer: (B) is not eligible to make any further remittance under the Scheme during that financial year.

Once a remittance is made for an amount up to USD 2,50,000 during the financial year, a resident individual is not eligible to make any further remittance under the Scheme, even if the proceeds of the investments have been brought back into the country. The Scheme also does not envisage the extension of fund and non-fund based facilities by Authorised Dealer banks to resident individuals to facilitate capital account remittances, though such facilities may be extended to facilitate current account remittances.
